meta.title: Roster — An office for your coding agents
meta.description: Your coding agents as little colleagues in a pixel office on your Mac — Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Codex. They walk to your desk when they're done. Free, open source, local-only.

hero.title: Your coding agents just got <mark>an office</mark>.
hero.subtitle: Roster turns every coding session — Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor or Codex — into a little colleague in a pixel office on your Mac. They work at their desks, stand up when they need you, and walk over to yours the moment the job is done.
hero.note: macOS 14+ · Signed & notarized · No account, no telemetry
hero.caption: Live from the room — the agents take turns walking over when they finish.

positioning.title: Stop babysitting terminals.
positioning.body: You kick off an agent, alt-tab to real work, and lose track — done ten minutes ago? Stuck on a question? Lists, diffs and kanban boards can tell you, if you remember to go read them. Roster is the ambient version: a quiet little office in the corner of your screen. You don't read it, you glance at it. The state of the room is the state of your agents.

features.title: A room that speaks for itself

f1.title: The walk
f1.body: Real work earns a crossing: when an agent finishes a long task, it stands up, walks across the office and waits at your desk until you've had a look — with a native notification (and a ding) in case you're elsewhere. Never find out twenty minutes late again.

f2.title: One glance, every state
f2.body: Seated and working. Standing when it needs your input. Walking when it's done. At your desk for review. A red pill when a turn fails. And each desk wears its tool's logo, so a mixed office reads at a glance.

f3.title: Click a colleague
f3.body: Click an agent — in the room or in the sidebar — and its profile card slides in: the last thing it said, the repo path, one button for VS Code, one for the Terminal, one to mark the work reviewed.

f4.title: A real little office
f4.body: The colleagues are real 3D — voxel bodies under a real light, turning toward wherever they walk. Stroll around with the arrow keys (the camera stays glued to you, Gather-style), double-click to hurry somewhere, zoom when the room gets crowded.

how.title: Three small pieces, all local

s1.title: A hook
s1.body: With your consent, Roster wires every agent it finds: hooks in each Claude Code and Gemini CLI settings, Cursor's hooks.json, Codex's notify — every config backed up first. From then on, each session event lands in a local spool file.

s2.title: A spool file
s2.body: Events pile up even while Roster is closed. On launch the room replays them and catches up — no server, no socket, no polling.

s3.title: A room
s3.body: Events map one-to-one to the choreography: needs-input stands the agent up, a finished long turn triggers the walk, a failure pulls it back to its station, and a closed session takes its desk along.

how.privacy: Everything stays on your Mac. Roster never reads your code — only session events. No network, no account, no telemetry.

open.title: MIT, from day one
open.body: Roster is free and open source. The state machine is unit-tested, the fragile parts are isolated behind a thin layer, and every design decision is written down in the repo — including the verified research behind the multi-agent support (docs/providers.md). Good first issues are waiting for you.

q1.q: Which coding agents does it work with?
q1.a: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor and Codex, out of the box. Roster detects the tools installed on your Mac and wires them all with one click — each config backed up first. opencode is next on the list; the research is public in docs/providers.md.

q2.a: No. It only sees session events: state changes, the working directory, and the last assistant message for the summary. Nothing ever leaves your machine.

q3.q: Why isn't it on the Mac App Store?
q3.a: Roster needs to read your agents' config folders (~/.claude, ~/.gemini, …) and install its hooks there, which the App Store sandbox forbids. It ships as a signed, notarized DMG on GitHub Releases instead.

q4.q: What if a tool changes its file formats?
q4.a: The hooks and notify mechanisms Roster relies on are documented interfaces, so the core is safe. The undocumented parts — transcript scanning — are isolated and fail silently; worst case, the room misses a warm start. And when something drifts, the fix is one automatic update away.

cta.title: Give your agents a desk.
cta.body: One DMG, one click — and your coding sessions become colleagues, whichever agent runs them.

footer.tagline: A little office for your coding agents. They walk to your desk when they're done.
